name: tabs
title: Tabs
description: Several panels, one shown at a time, chosen from a row of tabs.

behavior.summary: A `tablist` of `tab` buttons over a set of `tabpanel` regions, with roving tabindex and arrow-key movement along the declared axis. Every tab points at its panel and every panel back at its tab, which is the pairing that makes a tablist a tablist.

decisions.decision: Which of three, when they all look like one bar of options
decisions.why: Three components here can look like one enclosed bar of options, so each one's contract says which is which. SegmentedControl is a question with a short fixed set of answers: single, always filled, cannot be cleared. ToggleButtonGroup is the same ARIA pattern with a wider API — multiple selection, deselection, vertical orientation, the toggle-button variants — so reach for it when you need any of those. Tabs is a different pattern entirely: tabs reveal a region, each naming a panel and each panel naming its tab, and if what is being chosen is which content is shown rather than what gets submitted, it is Tabs — which can be drawn to look exactly like the other two and is still announced as a tablist.

decisions.decision: It is not a segmented control, though it can be drawn as one
decisions.why:
`SegmentedControl` is the component for that, and the two are not the same control however they are painted. A segmented control picks a VALUE: it is a radiogroup, every option is announced as a choice, and the answer is submitted with the rest of the form. Tabs reveal a REGION: moving between them changes what is on screen rather than what will be sent. Using one for the other is not a style error — a radiogroup standing in for tabs tells a screen reader a form is being filled in, and tabs standing in for a form control hide the answer inside a region nobody submits.

That is entirely about the ROLE. `variant="segmented"` draws a tablist to look like the segmented control, which is a legitimate design choice and changes nothing announced. The cost is only that a reader cannot tell the two apart by eye; assistive technology still can.

decisions.decision: Activation is the caller's choice, because it has a cost
decisions.why: Automatic — the arrow keys select as they move — is what APG recommends and what a reader expects, but arrowing past four tabs then renders four panels. Manual moves focus and waits for Enter or Space, which is right when a panel fetches something. The wrong one is not cosmetic: automatic over an expensive panel fires requests nobody asked for.

decisions.decision: An items array rather than children
decisions.why: The component owns the id wiring that makes a tablist a tablist — every tab pointing at its panel, every panel back at its tab — and that is the error-prone part. Handing it out to be assembled would mean cloning elements to inject ids, and a mis-wired pair looks perfectly fine on screen. The trade is that a tab is a label and some content rather than arbitrary structure; if that stops being enough the API should change rather than the caller working around it.

decisions.decision: Every panel stays mounted, all but one hidden
decisions.why: Unmounting would throw away whatever state each panel held — a half-filled form, a scroll position, an expanded row — every time the reader glanced at another tab. `hidden` keeps them out of the accessibility tree and out of the tab order without destroying them.

decisions.decision: A panel is in the tab order even with nothing focusable inside it
decisions.why: Without `tabIndex={0}` on the panel, Tab from the tablist skips a panel of plain text entirely and the reader never reaches the content the tab just promised them.

items.summary: The tabs and their panels, in the order they are read.
use: Two to about six panels of one thing seen different ways: an invoice's details, its history, its notes.
dont: Steps in a sequence. Tabs are peers a reader moves between freely; a process with an order and a completion state is not this.
One tab. A tablist of one is a heading with extra keyboard behaviour.
Navigation between pages. These are regions of one page — a destination belongs in a nav, where it has an address.
items.a11y: Each entry becomes a `tab` pointing at its `tabpanel` with `aria-controls`, and the panel points back with `aria-labelledby`. The selected tab carries `aria-selected`; the rest are `hidden`, which keeps them out of both the accessibility tree and the tab order.

value.summary: Which panel is showing. Makes the component controlled.
use: Driving the selection from a URL, so a tab can be linked to and survives a reload.

defaultValue.summary: Starting panel for uncontrolled tabs. Defaults to the first.
use: Opening on something other than the first panel.

onValueChange.summary: Called with the panel that should be shown.
use: Loading a panel's data the first time it is opened.
dont: Assuming it fires once per tab. Under automatic activation it fires for every tab the arrow keys pass through — which is the reason `activation` exists.

use: Naming what the tabs divide: "Invoice" for a set covering one invoice's details, history and notes.
dont: The word "tabs", which the role already says.
label.a11y: Becomes the tablist's `aria-label`. Required unless `labelledBy` names an element — a tablist with no name is announced as a bare tablist.

labelledBy.summary: Names the tablist from an element the reader can see.
use: Pointing at the heading the tabs sit under, so the name changes with it.
dont: Passing it alongside `label` and expecting both. This one wins, and never renders the other.
labelledBy.a11y: Wins over `label`, because it points at text on screen.

orientation.summary: Which axis the tabs run along.
use: `vertical` for a long set, or beside a wide panel.
dont: `vertical` for two or three short tabs, where a row is easier to scan.
orientation.a11y: Announced as `aria-orientation`, and it decides which arrow keys move: left/right on the horizontal axis, up/down on the vertical. Announcing it is a promise the component keeps.

activation.summary: Whether the arrow keys select as they move.
use: `automatic` — the default, and what a reader expects — when the panels are already on the client.
`manual` when opening a panel costs something: a request, a render nobody asked for.
dont: `automatic` over panels that fetch. Arrowing across four tabs fires four requests, and the reader wanted the fifth.
activation.a11y: Both are conforming. `manual` moves focus and waits for Enter or Space; `automatic` selects as focus moves. A disabled tab is reachable either way — this system's disabled controls stay focusable — and selection does not follow focus onto it.

variant.summary: How the tablist is drawn. Appearance only.
use: `underline` — the default — for a wider set, or tabs of uneven length: the marker scales where an enclosed bar starts to crowd.
`segmented` for two to four short, peer-like tabs, where one enclosed bar reads as a single control.
dont: Reaching for `segmented` to make a form control. If the thing being chosen gets submitted, it is a `ToggleButtonGroup` — the appearance is available here, but the semantics are not interchangeable.
Mixing both appearances on one screen. They are the same control drawn two ways, and alternating them reads as two different mechanisms.
variant.a11y: Changes nothing: the roles, the keyboard model, the naming and `aria-selected` are identical either way. Under `segmented` the filled segment is the visual indicator instead of the marker bar, and the state is still announced, so it is not carried by colour alone. What it does cost is that a segmented tablist and a real segmented control are hard to tell apart by eye — they remain correctly distinguishable to a screen reader.

className.summary: Extra classes on the wrapper, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Constraining the width, or spacing the set from what surrounds it.
dont: Making it look like a segmented control. They are different controls, and looking alike is how they get used for each other.

usage.when: The commonest case: panels of the same subject, all already loaded.
usage.example:
<Tabs
  label="Invoice"
  items={[
    { value: "details", label: "Details", content: <Details /> },
    { value: "history", label: "History", content: <History /> },
    { value: "notes", label: "Notes", content: <Notes /> },
  ]}
/>
usage.notes: Automatic activation, which is the default: the panels are on the client, so selecting as the arrows move costs nothing and is what a reader expects.

usage.case: Panels that cost something to open
usage.when: A panel fetches, so arrowing past it must not.
usage.example:
<Tabs
  label="Invoice"
  activation="manual"
  value={tab}
  onValueChange={(next) => {
    setTab(next);
    load(next);
  }}
  items={items}
/>
usage.notes: `manual` is the whole point here: under automatic, arrowing from the first tab to the fourth fires three requests for panels nobody wanted to see. Controlled as well, so the tab can come from the URL and survive a reload.

usage.when: Two to four short tabs, where one enclosed bar reads as a single control.
usage.example:
<Tabs
  label="Range"
  variant="segmented"
  items={[
    { value: "week", label: "Week", content: <Week /> },
    { value: "month", label: "Month", content: <Month /> },
  ]}
/>
usage.notes: Appearance only — this is still a tablist revealing regions, and still announced as one. Worth stating because the same shape built from `SegmentedControl` would be a radiogroup answering a question, and the two are not interchangeable however alike they look. If the panels were empty, that would be the tell that this is the wrong one.

usage.case: Don't: tabs standing in for a segmented control
usage.when: Never — this is the shape to recognise and avoid.
usage.notes: Don't. Empty panels are the tell: nothing is being revealed, so this is a question being answered — `SegmentedControl`, which is what that component is for. Tabs tell a screen reader that regions are being shown and hidden, and the answer here would sit inside a region nobody submits.

base.summary: The set, in either appearance. `underline` reads as an edge with a marker on it; `segmented` reads as one enclosed bar. The segmented form borrows the tokens the real segmented control uses rather than picking its own, so the two cannot drift into looking nearly-but-not-quite alike.

tab.summary: One tab. The resting tone is the secondary text colour, so the selected one reads as emphasised rather than the rest reading as dimmed.

tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

tab-selected.summary: The panel you are looking at. Marked twice over: the bar is the visual cue and aria-selected is the announced one, so the state is never carried by colour alone.

tokens.indicator: theme.accent-role.bg at border.2, straddling the list's rule so the tab reads as joined to its panel

panel.summary: The region a tab reveals. Focusable even with nothing focusable inside, so Tab from the tablist reaches it.

tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

variant-segmented.summary: The enclosed bar, sized to its content rather than to the container — the real segmented control is inline-flex and hugs its options, and a tablist drawn to resemble it should do the same. No marker: the filled segment is the indicator, which is why the underline's marker is scoped away here. The selection is still announced through aria-selected.

tokens.track background: theme.bg.muted — exactly what that step is documented for: the most recessed background, an inset well or a track. No border: a track sitting a real step below what it is on does not need an edge drawn round it.
tokens.bar sizing: align-self to its content, while the panel still fills the width
